real_title: R (on the application of Quaye) v Secretary of State for Justice
anonymised_title: R (Appellant) v Secretary of State for Justice
appeal_from: Court of Appeal (Civil Division) (England and Wales) [2025] EWCA Civ 226
facts:
The Appellant, aged 17 years and 9 months, and a 15-year-old co-defendant took knives to a party and fatally stabbed a man. The Appellant was convicted of murder in November 2014, when he was 18. He was sentenced on 16 January 2015, aged 18 years and 5 months, to detention during His Majesty's pleasure (DHMP), the mandatory sentence for murder committed under 18. The judge fixed a minimum term of 15 years, after which release depends on the Parole Board. The co-defendant, still a child, received the same sentence and minimum term.

Since 30 November 2000 the minimum term has been fixed by the sentencing judge. Before that the Secretary of State fixed it. After 2000 the Secretary of State operated a policy, as an act of clemency, under which a detainee could apply for a reduction in the minimum term at the halfway point, based on exceptional progress in custody. That policy applied when the offence was committed and when the Appellant was sentenced. From 18 February 2021 a revised policy removed eligibility for those aged 18 or over at sentence. The Appellant does not challenge that revision.

In 2022 Parliament inserted sections 27A and 27B into the Crime (Sentences) Act 1997. Only a person under 18 when sentenced may apply for a minimum term review, after serving half the minimum term. The High Court decides the review, and section 27A(11) provides that there is no other right to a review. The Appellant reached the halfway point on 15 March 2022. He could not apply, but his co-defendant could.

On 8 September 2022 the Appellant brought judicial review proceedings seeking declarations of incompatibility under section 4 of the Human Rights Act 1998. He relied on articles 5, 7, and 14 (read with article 5) of the ECHR. The Divisional Court held that the provisions were incompatible with article 5 and with article 14 read with article 5. It did not decide the article 7 claim and dismissed an article 6 claim, which is not pursued. It made declarations of incompatibility. The Secretary of State appealed to the Court of Appeal, which allowed the appeal and quashed the declarations. It dismissed the Appellant's cross-appeal on article 7. The Appellant appeals to the Supreme Court.

issues.question: Does the exclusion, by section 27A of the Crime (Sentences) Act 1997, of any right to a minimum term review for persons aged 18 or over when sentenced to detention during His Majesty's pleasure give rise to a risk of arbitrary detention contrary to article 5 ECHR?

Is the difference in treatment between persons sentenced to detention during His Majesty's pleasure when under 18 and those sentenced when aged 18 or over, as regards the right to apply for a minimum term review under section 27A, without objective and reasonable justification, so as to be incompatible with article 14 read with article 5 ECHR?

Does removal of the opportunity to apply for a minimum term review for those aged 18 or over when sentenced impose a heavier penalty than the one applicable when the offence was committed, contrary to article 7(1) ECHR?

appellant_submissions:
Article 5: detention that is lawful in domestic law may still be arbitrary. Denying any possibility of review of the minimum term risks unnecessary or excessive detention. DHMP has an inherent feature of continuing review, as recognised in Venables and Thompson and Smith, so that detainees can be released when it is judged appropriate. Removing review means some offenders will serve longer than they lawfully should.

Article 14 with article 5: the Appellant and his co-defendant are in an analogous position and differ only in age at sentence. Child offenders should not be treated as adults, and the critical age is age at the offence. Minimum term reviews are the means by which the welfare of child offenders is respected in mandatory indefinite sentences, and R (SC) supports a more intense review where children's best interests are involved. Maturation continues beyond 18. The complaint concerns arbitrary detention, so close scrutiny is required (Clift). The measure operates retrospectively, defeating the legitimate expectation of those who had already made exceptional progress. Section 27A is not a justified bright line, and the Divisional Court was right to give little weight to the victims' families' interests.

Article 7: section 27A, six years after sentence, makes the provisional and reducible tariff immutable. It transforms DHMP into an adult mandatory life sentence in all but name. Del Río Prada and Kupinskyy show that such a change affects the scope of the penalty, not merely its execution. The foreseeability requirement applies.
respondent_submissions:
Article 5: the minimum term was lawfully fixed by the sentencing judge under section 82A after proper procedure and was open to appeal. Saadi and James show that for article 5(1)(a) the length of a sentence with a causal link to a conviction is for national authorities, absent bad faith or similar grounds. No Strasbourg authority requires every indeterminate sentence imposed on a child to be reviewable. Since section 82A, continuing review is no longer inherent in DHMP, and the Secretary of State's earlier review policy was an act of clemency.

Article 14: any difference in treatment is justified. The aim is to reduce distress to victims' families, who are contacted and may submit new statements every time a review is sought, as the 2020 White Paper explained. Parliament drew a clear line at 18 at sentence, which reflects the law's general treatment of adults and children, and the child sentencing guidelines still apply fully. A wide margin of appreciation applies: this is primary legislation on penal and social policy, age is not a suspect ground, and there is no European consensus. Parliament considered and rejected an amendment to raise the cut-off to 26. Since February 2021 the Revised Policy had already removed review for this group, so nothing further was lost. There was no legal right to an executive review, and transitional provision was made.

Article 7: review concerned early release and the execution of the sentence, not the penalty (Hogben, Kafkaris, Morgan). The sentence remains indefinite with a court-set minimum term and the possibility of release, so Del Río Prada and Kupinskyy are distinguishable.
legal_materials:
Crime (Sentences) Act 1997, s 27A(1)-(2): a person serving a DHMP sentence who was under 18 when sentenced may apply for a minimum term review after serving half the minimum term. Section 27A(11): no right to request a review of the minimum term other than under s 27A. Section 27B: the High Court may reduce or confirm the minimum term, taking account of exceptional rehabilitation and serious risk to welfare or rehabilitation.

Powers of Criminal Courts (Sentencing) Act 2000, s 82A (court fixes the minimum term); Sentencing Act 2020, s 259; Children and Young Persons Act 1933, s 44 (welfare principle); Police, Crime, Sentencing and Courts Act 2022, s 128(3)-(4) (transitional provision).

ECHR art 5(1)(a); art 7(1) (no heavier penalty than that applicable at the time of the offence); art 14 (non-discrimination).

Authorities: R v SSHD ex p Venables and Thompson [1998] AC 407; R (Smith) v SSHD [2006] 1 AC 159; V v United Kingdom (1999) 30 EHRR 121; Saadi v UK (2008) 47 EHRR 17; James v UK (2012) 56 EHRR 12; Clift v UK (2010); Kafkaris v Cyprus (2008); Del Río Prada v Spain (2013); Kupinskyy v Ukraine (2022); Morgan v Ministry of Justice [2023] UKSC 14; R (SC) v SSWP [2021] UKSC 26; Bank Mellat (No 2) [2013] UKSC 39.
actual_reasoning_summary: The Court held that section 82A of the 2000 Act had fundamentally changed DHMP, so continuing review of the minimum term was no longer an inherent feature of the sentence. Sections 27A and 27B put minimum term reviews on an entirely statutory footing. Article 5 was not breached, because the minimum term was lawfully fixed by the court, had a sufficient causal link to the conviction, and Strasbourg case law does not require such a term to be reviewable. On article 14 read with article 5, the Court applied a wide margin of appreciation and its own fresh proportionality assessment. The legitimate aim of reducing distress to victims' families was served by a bright line at age 18 at sentence, in primary legislation that Parliament had considered carefully. Retrospectivity carried little weight, because the Revised Policy had already removed the opportunity and there was no right to an executive review. Article 7 was not engaged, because review concerned early release and the execution of the sentence rather than the penalty itself, which remains an indefinite sentence with a court-fixed minimum term.
outcome_evidence: Para 145: "For all these reasons, sections 27A and 27B of the 1997 Act are compatible with articles 5, 7 and 14 read with article 5 of the ECHR. ... The difference in treatment provided for by section 27A is objectively justified. Accordingly, we would dismiss the appeal." (Lord Stephens and Lady Simler, with whom Lord Sales, Lord Briggs and Lord Hamblen agree.)
